nameStory: The name "bobolink" comes from the male's distinctive bubbling song that sounds like "bob-o-link, bob-o-link, spink, spank, spink." Early settlers thought the bird was literally saying its own name! An older name for this species was "rice bird" because flocks would descend on rice fields during migration, sometimes causing significant crop damage.
description: The bobolink is a sparrow-sized songbird and member of the blackbird family, about the size of a red-winged blackbird. Males in breeding plumage are striking with their bold black-and-white pattern, while females and non-breeding males are streaky brown and blend in with grasslands. They're known for their remarkable migration, flying thousands of miles from New England grasslands to spend winter in South America. These birds are grassland specialists that prefer open meadows and fields.

idTips.label: Male breeding plumage
idTips.description: Males in spring and early summer wear a distinctive "backwards tuxedo" - jet black below with bright white patches on the back and shoulders, plus a creamy yellow-buff patch on the back of the head that looks like a golden cap

idTips.label: Female and fall male appearance
idTips.description: Streaky brown birds with warm buff-yellow underparts and bold dark stripes through the eye and crown, resembling large sparrows but with a distinctly pointed bill

idTips.label: Bubbling song
idTips.description: Males produce a liquid, tinkling song that sounds like water bubbling over rocks, often delivered while hovering or perched on tall grass stems - once heard, never forgotten

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive undulating pattern, flashing white wing patches (in males), often in small flocks that seem to roll through the air like waves

idTips.label: Sharp, pointed bill
idTips.description: More pointed and finch-like than other blackbirds, adapted for eating small seeds and insects picked from grass stems and flower heads

habitat: Look for bobolinks in large, open grasslands, hayfields, and meadows, especially those that aren't mowed until late summer. They prefer areas with tall grasses mixed with wildflowers and avoid heavily grazed pastures. You'll find them in river valleys, abandoned fields, and grassland preserves throughout New England, though they've become much less common as hayfields have disappeared.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive in May wearing their stunning breeding plumage and immediately begin their bubbling territorial songs from prominent perches. This is the best time to spot and identify them as they're most visible and vocal.
seasonality.summer: Breeding season continues through July, with males still in their distinctive black-and-white plumage. Females are busy nesting low in the grass and are much harder to spot.
seasonality.fall: Males molt into streaky brown plumage similar to females, making identification much more challenging. They form flocks and quietly feed in grasslands before beginning their epic migration south.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these remarkable travelers spend winter in the grasslands of Paraguay, Argentina, and Bolivia, making them one of our longest-distance migrants.

funFact: Bobolinks make one of the longest migrations of any songbird in the Western Hemisphere, flying roughly 12,500 miles roundtrip from New England breeding grounds to South American wintering areas - that's like flying halfway around the Earth every year!
confusionNotes: Female and fall male bobolinks are often confused with large sparrows or female red-winged blackbirds, but bobolinks have more pointed bills, more contrasting face stripes, and warmer buff-yellow underparts. Remember: if it looks like a big, elegant sparrow in a grassland, it's probably a bobolink.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "blackbird," bobolinks are only black during male breeding season and are more closely related to orioles than true blackbirds. Their old nickname "rice bird" made them agricultural pests historically, leading to massive hunting pressure that contributed to their decline alongside habitat loss.
compareHints: Bobolinks are the only members of their genus, making them unique among New World blackbirds. Compared to their closest relatives like red-winged blackbirds and meadowlarks, bobolinks are distinguished by the male's reversed color pattern (black below, white above) and their exclusive grassland habitat. Unlike meadowlarks which have yellow breasts, bobolinks have streaky brown females and striking black-and-white males.
